Issued at 245 AM CDT Thu Aug 6 2026

Early Thursday morning satellite captures mostly clear skies over 
the southern half of MN and western WI. Farther south, GOES 
nighttime RGB channel displays a wall of dense fog that has 
developed over the northern half of Iowa. Neighboring WFO's DMX/ARX 
have issued a Dense Fog Advisory that extends to the MN/IA border. 
Through 2 AM, only a few surface observations south of I-90 in MN 
have reported brief visibility reductions of less than 1 mile. For 
now, we've opted to hold off on a headline, but observational trends 
in the near term may warrant a Special Weather Statement or Dense 
Fog Advisory for the southernmost tier of counties along I-90. Any 
fog that develops will erode shortly after daybreak. 

The main driver of our weather over the coming days is an active jet 
positioned across southern Canada. Surface winds across MN have 
turned southerly in response to a lead shortwave that is currently 
pivoting eastward across central Manitoba. Mid-level warm air 
advection out of the northern Plains is increasing, which will yield 
a slightly warmer day with highs in the low to mid 80s. Southerly 
winds may gust between 25-30 mph across western MN as high 
pressure builds eastward and the the pressure gradient tightens 
ahead of our next frontal passage on Friday. In addition to 
warmer temperatures and upcoming precipitation chances, the 
active northwesterly jet will also be responsible for the 
transportation of wildfire smoke from the Pacific Northwest 
across the northern CONUS later today. Strong agreement across 
smoke bearing CAMs supported boosting sky cover in the grids to 
capture the hazy appearance of the anticipated high concentration
of incoming wildfire smoke aloft. The good news is that the smoke
particulates are forecast to remain elevated, which will keep 
surface air quality in the Good/Moderate categories per the 
latest forecast from MPCA.

Over the next 24-36 hours, a stronger secondary shortwave will dig 
across Manitoba and spawn a surface low pressure system that is 
forecast to move northeast across Ontario prior to occluding and 
taking residence over Hudson Bay late Friday. While the main lobe of 
synoptic forcing will remain well to the north of the International 
Border, the system's trailing cold front will extend well south into 
the Upper Midwest and be the focal point for showers and thunderstorms
on Friday. CAMs have advertised isolated shower chances within a wing
of strengthening warm advection across eastern SD and far west-central
MN later this evening, however forecast soundings reveal dry air
and capping, so have collaborated with western neighbors to keep
the forecast grids dry until Friday morning. Our latest forecast
includes 20-30 PoPs across southwestern MN from daybreak through
mid-morning, though confidence in coverage of precipitation 
during the first part of Friday is on the lower side. By midday 
and beyond, PoPs begin to increase (40-60%) as HREF/REFS CAM 
clusters capture the anticipated development of scattered 
showers and thunderstorms ahead of the cold front, which is 
progged to approach the I-35 corridor from the northwest early 
Friday afternoon. Communities along and east of I-35 in eastern 
MN/western WI are located within a Day 2 Marginal Risk (Level 
1/5) from SPC. The pre-frontal environment will be lacking a 
bit in the shear department, but moisture pooling ahead of the 
boundary will yield 1500+ J/kg of CAPE. The instability combined
with a plume of steep lapse rates (7.5-8C/km) will support a 
few stronger storms as they grow upscale into a broken line 
Friday afternoon. The primary severe weather hazards will be 
isolated instances of damaging wind (60+ mph) and large hail 
(1"+). Storm chances end by mid-evening or so across western WI.

Northwesterly flow will continue to be the main influence over the 
forecast through the weekend. A remnant baroclinic zone is forecast 
to bisect the Upper Midwest from northwest to southeast, serving as 
a dividing line between cooler Canadian air to the north and much 
warmer air sourced from ridging over the desert southwest. In 
addition, the mid-level temperature gradient will provide the tracks 
for additional precipitation chances through the weekend and into 
early next week. Latest trends continue to support highs in the low 
to mid 80s Saturday and Sunday. We'll watch wildfire smoke trends
to the west as the concentration of smoke aloft may also have 
an impact on surface heating. In the precipitation department, 
the NBM features PoPs across southern MN Saturday evening tied 
to a weak subtle shortwave forecast to slide out of the Plains 
into Iowa. Better chances for showers and storms will be tied to
a slightly stronger wave set to move from the Dakotas into 
MN/WI Sunday PM through Monday AM. Near normal temperatures in 
the upper 70s/low 80s follow for much of next week.
